Let your fingertips just hook under the bar, the shoulders hold it, not the hands. Sit straight down, elbows stay high the whole time. If the elbows drop, the bar rolls forward: rack it and go lighter.

alts.name: Walking Lunge
alts.cue: Step forward into each lunge and keep travelling. Harder on balance and on the front knee. 8/leg.

alts.name: Cossack Squat
alts.cue: The deeper version. Same sideways sit, but let the straight leg's toes come up and go as low as you can. Bodyweight first, hold a dumbbell at the chest when it is easy. 3x6/side.

alts.name: DB Step-Up
alts.cue: Bench at knee height, drive through the heel of the top foot. 8/leg.

exercises.name: DB Reverse Fly
exercises.cue: Standing, in the rest between sets of the lift above. A dumbbell in each hand. Push your hips back and lean your chest forward to about 45 degrees, roughly halfway to parallel with the floor, back flat, eyes down. Let the dumbbells hang straight below your chest with a small bend in the elbows. Now open your arms out to the SIDES like opening a pair of curtains, until your hands are level with your shoulders. Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the top, then lower slowly. Success looks like: your torso does not rise as you lift, and you feel it between the shoulder blades rather than in your lower back. Go light, this is a small muscle. First time out, pick a weight you are sure you could lift 15 times and stop at 12.
exercises.whyHere: The reverse fly goes in the rest because the back of the shoulder takes no part in a lunge.

alts.name: Cable Reverse Fly
alts.cue: Standing, in the rest between sets of the lift above. At the adjustable cable column, standing tall, a handle in each hand and a small bend in the elbows. Now open your arms out to the SIDES like opening a pair of curtains, until your hands are level with your shoulders. Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the top, then lower slowly. Success looks like: your torso does not rise as you lift, and you feel it between the shoulder blades rather than in your lower back. Go light, this is a small muscle. First time out, pick a weight you are sure you could lift 15 times and stop at 12.

alts.name: Chest-Supported Reverse Fly
alts.cue: Same movement lying face down on an incline bench, which removes the lower back entirely. Use this if the standing version makes your back ache.

blocks.why: One leg at a time, first in the session, which is the fresh slot this pattern never used to get. Six to twelve reps a leg, so it is heavier per leg than its other exposure. The reverse fly goes in the rest because the back of the shoulder takes no part in a lunge.

blocks.label: Horizontal Press

exercises.name: DB Incline Press
exercises.cue: SET THE BENCH ONE OR TWO NOTCHES UP FROM FLAT, about 30 degrees, not half way up. This is what you have been doing since at least 28 August and the card was still saying flat, so your logged weights come with you and nothing resets. THE DIFFERENCE, since you asked in the note box: neither one is better. Flat works the middle and lower chest, an incline works the top of the chest and more front shoulder, and they are two halves of the same muscle. The steeper you go the more the shoulder takes over, which is why one or two notches and no more. Success looks like: you feel it across your collarbone rather than under your nipple line. If the shoulders are doing all of it, drop the bench a notch. Feet flat on the floor. Pull your shoulder blades back and down into the bench and keep them there, like you are pinching a pencil between them. Breathe in, lower the dumbbells until you feel a good stretch across the chest, PAUSE for one second so there is no bounce, then press up and breathe out. The dumbbells travel slightly toward each other at the top but do not clang. ADDED 2026-08-22, after he reported feeling this mostly in the triceps and the front of the shoulder: that is usually where the dumbbells are travelling, not how hard you are pushing. Two things to try. Before the first rep, pull your shoulder blades DOWN and TOGETHER into the bench and keep them pinned there the whole set, so your chest is the highest point and the shoulders cannot roll forward. Then press over your LOWER chest, not your collarbone: at the bottom the dumbbells should be beside your nipples with your elbows about halfway between tucked-in and straight-out, and at the top they finish above the same spot rather than drifting toward your face. Success looks like: at the bottom you feel a stretch across the chest, not a pinch at the front of the shoulder. This is standard coaching practice, not a trial finding.

alts.name: Machine Chest Press
alts.cue: Your second press of the week, moderate rather than heavy: Tuesday is the day the bench gets pushed. Machine on purpose, so a tired chest does not have to balance dumbbells. Set the seat so the handles line up with the MIDDLE of your chest. Press out until the arms are straight without locking hard, then come back slowly until you feel the stretch. Shoulder blades stay pinned back against the pad.

alts.name: Assisted Dip
alts.cue: Lean your chest forward to bias the chest. Enough counterweight for 8 clean reps. You had 5 strict dips in May, so this is trackable.

alts.name: Chest Fly Machine
alts.cue: Elbows slightly bent and fixed, bring the arms together in front of you and squeeze for one second. Stretch, not a press.

exercises.name: DB Calf Raise
exercises.cue: Standing on the floor in the rest between lunge sets, a dumbbell in each hand hanging at your sides. Feet about hip width. Push all the way up onto your toes, as high as you can go, and hold for one second at the top. Then lower slowly, about three seconds down, until your heels touch the floor and you feel a stretch through the back of the calf. Success looks like: you can hold the top position still for a second without wobbling, and the slow way down is what you feel most. If you cannot hold the top, the dumbbells are too heavy. This is the flat-floor version, so the stretch at the bottom is smaller than on the machine; that is the trade for it costing you no walk.
exercises.whyHere: The calf raise goes in the press rest because the calf takes no part in a press and you can do it standing right there.

alts.name: Machine Calf Raise
alts.cue: On the standing calf machine. Let the heels sink until you feel a stretch, pause one second at the bottom, then push all the way up onto your toes and squeeze for one second. Slow both directions. This is ankle insurance for the running.

blocks.why: The fresh slot for the chest, which you pointed out was a partner in every appearance and never anywhere near the front of a session. The calf raise goes in the press rest because the calf takes no part in a press and you can do it standing right there.

blocks.label: Horizontal Pull

exercises.name: BB Row
exercises.cue: This has been stuck at 165 lb since May because it always came fifth, when you were already cooked. It now leads the day, so it should move. Hinge forward until your chest is roughly parallel to the floor, knees slightly bent, back flat. Breathe in and brace. Pull the bar to your belly button by driving your ELBOWS backward past your ribs, then lower it all the way under control. Your torso does not move: if you are standing up a little to help the bar, it is too heavy.

alts.name: Lat Pulldown
alts.cue: Sit tall with your thighs locked under the pad. Start with your arms fully straight so you feel the stretch down your sides. Pull your ELBOWS down toward your ribs rather than thinking about your hands, and bring the bar to your upper chest. Let it back up slowly and all the way straight. Building toward real pull-ups.

alts.name: Straight-Arm Pulldown
alts.cue: This is your freestyle catch trained directly, which is why it stays even though the rest of the day changed. Cable set high, rope or straight bar, stand back a step and hinge slightly forward. Arms stay STRAIGHT the whole time, elbows barely bent and locked there. Sweep the bar down in an arc to your thighs and squeeze the muscles down the sides of your back, then let it float back up. Much lighter than a lat pulldown, because straight arms are a long lever.

alts.name: Chest-Supported DB Row
alts.cue: Chest on an incline bench, dumbbells hanging. The bench removes the lower back entirely, so nothing can cheat. Good on a day the RDLs left your back tired.

alts.name: Seated Cable Row
alts.cue: Tall chest, pull the handle to your stomach, squeeze the shoulder blades, let it stretch all the way forward.

alts.name: DB Pullover
alts.cue: Lying across or along a bench, one dumbbell held over the chest with near-straight arms. Lower it behind your head until you feel the stretch under the armpits, then pull it back over. 3x12.

alts.name: Assisted Pull-Up
alts.cue: Set the counterweight so you get 6 clean reps: full hang with straight arms at the bottom, chin over the bar at the top. Log the COUNTERWEIGHT, and remember it is the one number here that should go DOWN over time. When 6 feels easy, take 10 lb of assistance off.

exercises.name: Hanging Knee Raise
exercises.cue: Hang from the pull-up bar on top of the rack, arms straight, feet clear of the floor. Bring both knees up toward your chest, and at the top KEEP GOING for a couple of inches by curling your hips under you, as if you were trying to show someone the soles of your shoes. That last bit is the part your abdominals actually do: stopping when your thighs are level is hip work and they only hold on. Then lower under control until your legs are straight and you have come to a STOP before the next rep, so every one starts from still rather than from a swing. Success looks like: no swinging, and you feel it across the front of your stomach at the top rather than in the front of your hips the whole way. If you cannot stop the swing, do fewer reps. Ten a set, and when fifteen is easy, straighten the legs instead of adding weight. THIS CUE IS A DRAFT: nobody has read it standing at the bar. Use the note box and say what it should say.
exercises.whyHere: Hanging knee raises again, on the bar above the rack you are standing in, because you said you would rather hang than lie on the floor.

alts.name: Hollow Hold
alts.cue: Lower back pressed flat into the floor, arms overhead and legs straight and lifted, so your body makes a shallow banana. Bend the knees or keep arms at your sides if the back lifts. 3x20s.

blocks.why: The lighter of the two rows, ten to twelve reps rather than eight, so the same movement is trained at more than one weight. Hanging knee raises again, on the bar above the rack you are standing in, because you said you would rather hang than lie on the floor.

blocks.label: Lower Back

exercises.name: Lumbar Extension
exercises.cue: NEW, AND IT IS A DIFFERENT EXERCISE FROM THE ONE YOU HAVE BEEN DOING ON THIS MACHINE. Same frame, opposite instruction. On the back extension you have logged since June you hold your back FLAT and your hip does the moving. Here your hip stays put and your BACK does the moving. That is the only way anything in your gym trains the muscles either side of your spine as the thing that moves you rather than the thing that holds on. START WITH NO WEIGHT AT ALL, arms crossed on your chest, and do not add any until this is easy: the weights on your other back extension do not carry over, and starting there is how people hurt themselves on this. HOW TO SET UP. Same as the other one. Hip pad top edge just below your hip bones, ankles under the rollers, feet flat. HOW TO DO IT. Start standing tall in the frame. Let your upper back curl down first, then your middle back, then your lower back, one bit at a time, the way you would roll down a wall. Three seconds down, and only as far as is comfortable, which the first few times will be about half the range. Then reverse it: lower back first, then middle, then upper, until you are standing tall again. STOP AT TALL. Do not arch backwards past it. Success looks like: the work is low down, in a band across your waist, and the next day feels like a working ache rather than anything sharp. Ten to fifteen reps. STOP AND TELL ME if you get anything sharp, anything that shoots down a leg, or anything still there the next morning. This one is a draft written for you and you are the only person who can say whether it works, so use the note box under it after the first session either way.

alts.name: 45-Degree Back Extension
alts.cue: THIS IS HIP WORK, NOT LOWER-BACK WORK, and that is a correction to what this card used to imply. With your back held flat, the muscles that MOVE you here are your bum and the back of your thighs. Your lower back holds still, which is exactly what it does in a squat or a Romanian deadlift. Nothing in your gym trains the lower back as the muscle that moves, and there is a question about that on this exercise. HOW TO SET UP. The padded frame angled at about 45 degrees. Set the hip pad so its TOP EDGE sits just below your hip bones, on the top of your thigh, not on your belly. Too high and you cannot bend at the hip; too low and it digs in. Ankles under the two rollers, feet flat on the platform. Hug the dumbbell against your chest with both arms. HOW TO DO IT. Bend forward at the HIP, letting your upper body fold down toward the floor, until you feel a stretch down the back of your thighs. Keep your back FLAT the whole way, like a plank, never rounded into a C. Then squeeze your bum and drive back up until your body is one straight line from ankle to head, and STOP THERE. Do not carry on past straight into an arch. Two seconds down, one second up. Success looks like: your back never changes shape, and you feel it in your bum and the back of your thighs. If you feel a pinch in your lower back instead of a working ache in the bum, you either rounded on the way down or went past straight at the top. YOUR WEIGHTS SO FAR: 40 lb in June, 45 in July, 3x10 at 50 lb on 8 August. TEN TO FIFTEEN REPS, and go up 5 lb once you hit fifteen. The range is that wide on purpose: at ten to twelve, the next dumbbell up is a bigger jump than twelve good reps earns, so you would fail it and drop back every time.

alts.name: Single-Leg Glute Bridge
alts.cue: On the floor. Lie on your back, one heel planted close to your butt, the other leg lifted and held straight out. Push through the planted heel and lift your hips until your body is a straight line from knee to shoulder, then lower slowly. Success looks like: you feel it in the back of the planted thigh and the butt cheek, not in your lower back. If you feel your lower back, your hips went too high. 3x12 each side.

exercises.name: DB Hammer Curl
exercises.cue: Standing, in the rest between sets of the lift above. A dumbbell in each hand hanging by your sides, palms facing IN toward your thighs and STAYING that way the whole rep: that is what makes it a hammer curl instead of a normal curl. Pin your elbows against your ribs. Bend the elbow and bring the dumbbell up toward your shoulder, then lower it all the way until the arm is straight. Success looks like: your elbows have not travelled forward and your body has not swung to start the rep. If it swings, go lighter. First time out, pick a weight you are sure you could lift 15 times and stop at 12.
exercises.whyHere: the biceps fall from six sets to three

alts.name: DB Biceps Curl
alts.cue: Standing, dumbbells, elbows still at your sides, no swinging. Squeeze at the top, lower slowly.

alts.name: Cable Curl
alts.cue: Low cable with a straight or EZ attachment. The cable keeps tension on the muscle at every point, including the top where dumbbells go light. 3x12.

alts.name: Incline DB Curl
alts.cue: A dumbbell in each hand on the incline bench. Sit with the backs of your upper arms flat on the slanted pad and keep them there. Curl up until your forearms are vertical, squeeze, then lower ALL THE WAY until the arms are straight. The pad is the point: it makes swinging impossible, so the weight will feel heavier than a standing curl. Start lighter than you think.

alts.name: Kettlebell Curl
alts.cue: A kettlebell in each hand by the handle, same elbow-pinned curl. The weight hangs behind your hand, which makes the top half harder.

blocks.why: The second of the two lower-back slots, and two a week is what takes this muscle from nothing to a real dose. It is the only thing in the week that trains it: everything else, the squat, the row, the hinge, asks your lower back to hold still and never to move. No load until you tell me it is easy, and the old flat-back version is one tap away on the swap list. THIS IS THE BLOCK TO DROP IF THE CLOCK BEATS YOU, and the price is that your lower back gets nothing that week and the biceps fall from six sets to three.

friday.name: Session D
friday.title: Session D: squat and hinge, press after

blocks.label: Power Primer

exercises.name: Lateral Bound
exercises.cue: THREE OR FOUR BOUNDS A SIDE, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE SET. Not as many as you can. Same reason as the box jump on Monday: what you are training is how hard you can push off in one go, and a tired bound is a slow bound, which trains something else. More work means more SETS. HOW TO DO IT. Replaces the broad jump, which you swapped out every single time. This is the sideways explosive work you asked for. Stand on your LEFT leg. Push off it sideways and land on your RIGHT leg only, then FREEZE completely still for two seconds before going back. Land with the knee bent and pointing over your toes, never caving inward. Only jump as far as you can land and freeze. Success looks like: silent landing, no wobble, no second little hop to catch yourself. If you cannot freeze it, go shorter.

alts.name: Box Jump
alts.cue: THREE JUMPS A SET, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE SET. Not as many as you can: three, then stop and rest. This is the one exercise here where being tired makes it worse rather than better, because what you are training is how fast you leave the floor, and the fourth jump is always slower than the first. A slow jump is just a squat you did standing up. Five sets of three is fifteen jumps, and every one of them should feel like the first. HOW TO DO IT. Stand a forearm's length from the box. Swing the arms back, bend the knees about a quarter of the way, and jump ONTO the box. Land with both feet flat and knees bent, quietly. Then STEP down one foot at a time, never jump down. Success looks like: you hear almost nothing when you land, and you could hold the landing still for two seconds. If you land with a thud or stumble, the box is too high. If the third jump feels slower than the first, rest longer before the next set rather than pushing through.

alts.name: Single-Leg Glute Bridge
alts.cue: On the floor. Lie on your back, one heel planted close to your butt, the other leg lifted and held straight out. Push through the planted heel and lift your hips until your body is a straight line from knee to shoulder, then lower slowly. Success looks like: you feel it in the back of the planted thigh and the butt cheek, not in your lower back. If you feel your lower back, your hips went too high. 3x12 each side.

alts.name: Banded Lateral Walk
alts.cue: Fallback only, on a day the dumbbells are all taken. Band above the knees, half squat, step sideways keeping the band tight. 3x10/side.

alts.name: Lateral Line Hop
alts.cue: The easier version. Both feet together, hop side to side over a line on the floor, small and fast, staying on the balls of your feet. 3x15.

alts.name: Banded Hip Abduction
alts.cue: Short band above the knees, seated on a bench. Push the knees apart against the band and hold two seconds at the widest point, then let them come back slowly. Success looks like: you feel it on the outside of the hip, above and behind the hip bone. 3x15.

alts.name: Clamshell
alts.cue: On your side, short band above the knees, knees bent 90. Open the top knee like a clam without letting your hips roll backwards. Success looks like: your top hip stays stacked over the bottom one. If you have to roll back to open further, you have gone as far as it goes. 3x15 each side.

blocks.why: Three bounds a side and that is the whole set. THE SAME DOSE AS THE JUMPS, and the units hid it: five sets of three jumps is fifteen contacts, three sets of three a side is eighteen. What you are training is how hard you can push off in one go, and a tired bound is a slow bound. Neither counts toward the set total on this card, and neither one asks you to add reps.

blocks.label: Squat

exercises.name: Front Squat
exercises.cue: Your second squat of the week, deliberately light. This is the technique fix: because the bar sits on the FRONT of your shoulders, your body is forced upright and depth gets easier, which is exactly what a back squat struggles with. Bar across the front of your shoulders, elbows driven forward and UP so the upper arms are near parallel to the floor. Let your fingertips just hook under the bar, the shoulders hold it, not the hands. Sit straight down, elbows stay high the whole time. If the elbows drop, the bar rolls forward: rack it and go lighter.

alts.name: BB Back Squat
alts.cue: The lift we are progressing. Stance slightly wider than your hips with the toes turned out a little. Breathe IN and hold it, tighten your stomach like you are about to be poked, then sit down between your feet until the crease of your hip is below the top of your knee. Knees push out over your second toe, they do not fall inward. Stand up and breathe out at the top. Take a fresh breath and re-tighten before EVERY rep, not just the first.

alts.name: Bulgarian Split Squat
alts.cue: Dumbbells hanging at your sides. Put the top of your back foot on the bench, laces down. Your front foot should be far enough forward that at the bottom your front shin is straight up and down, not leaning forward over your toes. Lower until your back knee is close to the floor. Drive up through the FRONT heel. The back leg is a kickstand, it does not push.

alts.name: Reverse Lunge
alts.cue: Dumbbells hanging at your sides, standing tall. Step straight BACKWARD, long enough that the back knee drops toward the floor and the front shin stays roughly vertical. Push through the FRONT heel to stand back up. Stepping backward rather than forward keeps the load off the front knee.

alts.name: Walking Lunge
alts.cue: Step forward into each lunge and keep travelling. Harder on balance and on the front knee. 8/leg.

alts.name: Heavy Goblet Squat
alts.cue: Same upright effect with a dumbbell held at the chest, and no wrist or elbow demand at all. The easiest way to feel a deep upright squat.

alts.name: Leg Press
alts.cue: Feet shoulder width on the platform. Lower until your knees are near your chest without your lower back rounding off the pad, then press. Use this on a day your back is tired.

exercises.name: DB Hammer Curl
exercises.cue: Standing, in the rest between sets of the lift above. A dumbbell in each hand hanging by your sides, palms facing IN toward your thighs and STAYING that way the whole rep: that is what makes it a hammer curl instead of a normal curl. Pin your elbows against your ribs. Bend the elbow and bring the dumbbell up toward your shoulder, then lower it all the way until the arm is straight. Success looks like: your elbows have not travelled forward and your body has not swung to start the rep. If it swings, go lighter. First time out, pick a weight you are sure you could lift 15 times and stop at 12.
exercises.whyHere: The curl goes in the rest because the biceps take no part in a squat.

alts.name: DB Biceps Curl
alts.cue: Standing, dumbbells, elbows still at your sides, no swinging. Squeeze at the top, lower slowly.

alts.name: Cable Curl
alts.cue: Low cable with a straight or EZ attachment. The cable keeps tension on the muscle at every point, including the top where dumbbells go light. 3x12.

alts.name: Incline DB Curl
alts.cue: A dumbbell in each hand on the incline bench. Sit with the backs of your upper arms flat on the slanted pad and keep them there. Curl up until your forearms are vertical, squeeze, then lower ALL THE WAY until the arms are straight. The pad is the point: it makes swinging impossible, so the weight will feel heavier than a standing curl. Start lighter than you think.

alts.name: Kettlebell Curl
alts.cue: A kettlebell in each hand by the handle, same elbow-pinned curl. The weight hangs behind your hand, which makes the top half harder.

blocks.why: The lighter squat of the two, eight to ten reps against five to seven on the heavy one. Same movement, same bar, different weight. The curl goes in the rest because the biceps take no part in a squat.

blocks.label: Hinge

exercises.name: BB Romanian Deadlift
exercises.cue: The heavy hinge, the one we progress. Breathe IN and tighten your stomach. Bar stays touching your legs the whole way, shins vertical. Bend the knees slightly and then FREEZE them, then push your hips backward toward the wall behind you. Go down until you feel a strong stretch down the back of your thighs, usually around knee height, and no further. Squeeze your bum and snap the hips forward to stand up, breathing out at the top. If your lower back rounds you have gone too far down. STRAPS, because you asked on 18 August: yes, use them, and they will not cost you anything here. Do the first warm-up set with bare hands so you keep noticing what your grip is doing, then strap up for all four working sets. The hamstrings are what this lift is for, and stopping a set because the bar is slipping out of your fingers trains neither. Your grip is not being neglected either: the Farmer Carry on Friday and the Suitcase Carry on Monday are both held bare-handed and that is where grip is meant to be worked. This is standard coaching practice rather than something a trial has tested, so it is a convention, not evidence.

open.q: When you are standing in the rack with the bar loaded for Romanian deadlifts, can someone else still reach the pull-up bar above you? If they cannot, you are already blocking it, so you may as well use it between your own sets. Can they reach it?

Do you want hanging knee raises in the rests between your Romanian deadlift sets? Either add them, which takes your ab work from 7 sets a week to 10, or move ab sets you already do into that gap so the week does not get longer. Your abs are covered either way, so this is preference. Which?

AND THE PREMISE UNDERNEATH IT MOVED FURTHER THAN THE NUMBER DID. When this was asked, abdominals were the one muscle in the week failing its floor, so "more ab sets" carried an implied urgency. They are not any more: verified against scripts/gym-targets.mjs on 2026-09-03, abdominals clear the floor of 4 at 7 direct sets and sit under the target of 10 by 3, which is the same band as twelve other muscles. The option is still live and it is now a preference rather than a repair. Say that when it is put to him.

Left as an open question rather than answered, because the choice between adding 3 sets and moving 3 sets that are already in the week is his: it is a trade between total time in the gym and where the work sits, and neither the arithmetic nor the evidence decides it.

alts.name: Single-Leg RDL
alts.cue: Has sat at 40 lb since May, so this time the weight moves, not just the reps. One dumbbell in the hand OPPOSITE the standing leg. Stand on one leg with the knee slightly bent and frozen. Push the hip backward and let the free leg extend straight behind you like a see-saw, keeping your hips square to the floor: the back hip must not open toward the ceiling. Go until you feel the hamstring stretch, then stand and squeeze. Slow. Touch the bench with your free toe if you lose balance.

alts.name: 45-Degree Back Extension
alts.cue: On the 45 degree pad. Hinge down and squeeze your bum to come up. Hug a plate for load.

alts.name: DB Romanian Deadlift
alts.cue: Two heavy dumbbells in front of your thighs. Same hip push backward, same freeze in the knees.

alts.name: KB Swing
alts.cue: Same hip snap, done fast. Hike the bell back between your legs, then SNAP the hips forward so the bell floats to chest height. Arms do nothing. Start at 35 lb. 2x12.

alts.name: Smith RDL
alts.cue: Bar on rails so it cannot drift away from your legs. Useful for grooving the hinge when you are tired.

alts.name: B-Stance RDL
alts.cue: Back toe lightly touching the floor for balance, but almost all the weight on the front leg. Much easier to balance, so you can load it heavier.

exercises.name: DB Lateral Lunge
exercises.cue: This is the sideways movement you asked for, and it is loaded on purpose: unweighted band walks were shown to do little. Hold one dumbbell at your chest. Step wide to the LEFT and sit back into that left hip, keeping the right leg straight with the foot flat. Both feet stay pointing forward the whole time. Push off the left foot to come back. You should feel a stretch on the inside of the straight leg and work in the bent leg's hip. Start with a light dumbbell and a small step, then widen the step before you add weight.
exercises.whyHere: The sideways lunge goes in the rest because it is the only loaded sideways movement on the card and it shares nothing with a hinge.

alts.name: Front Squat
alts.cue: Your second squat of the week, deliberately light. This is the technique fix: because the bar sits on the FRONT of your shoulders, your body is forced upright and depth gets easier, which is exactly what a back squat struggles with. Bar across the front of your shoulders, elbows driven forward and UP so the upper arms are near parallel to the floor. Let your fingertips just hook under the bar, the shoulders hold it, not the hands. Sit straight down, elbows stay high the whole time. If the elbows drop, the bar rolls forward: rack it and go lighter.

alts.name: Cossack Squat
alts.cue: The deeper version. Same sideways sit, but let the straight leg's toes come up and go as low as you can. Bodyweight first, hold a dumbbell at the chest when it is easy. 3x6/side.

blocks.why: The lighter hinge, eight to ten reps against six to eight on the heavy one, and one of only three hamstring exposures in the week. The sideways lunge goes in the rest because it is the only loaded sideways movement on the card and it shares nothing with a hinge.

blocks.label: Overhead Press

exercises.name: Seated DB Overhead Press
exercises.cue: STANDING, not seated: that is the difference between this and the seated version in the alternatives, and it is why this needs no bench. Done second in the session from 2026-08-22, and the reason is in "Why this is here". Dumbbells at shoulder height, palms facing forward. Squeeze your bum and tighten your stomach BEFORE you press, so your ribs do not flare and your lower back does not arch. Press straight up until the arms are locked out with the dumbbells over the middle of your head, not in front of your face. Lower under control to the shoulders. Success looks like: your ribs stay down and you can hold the lockout still for a second. If your back arches to start the rep, go lighter.

alts.name: Machine Shoulder Press
alts.cue: Set the seat so the handles start at about shoulder height, not above your ears. Press up until your arms are straight without shrugging, and come back down slowly until the handles are level with your shoulders again. Stop the set when your lower back starts arching off the pad.

alts.name: Half-Kneeling Single-Arm Press
alts.cue: One knee down, the other foot forward, one dumbbell in the hand on the SAME side as the down knee. Press it straight overhead without letting your ribs flare or your body lean away. It is two exercises at once: a press, and your trunk refusing to bend sideways under a load held on one side. Lighter than the two-dumbbell version by a lot, and that is the point.

alts.name: Seated DB Overhead Press
alts.cue: Bench upright, back supported. Takes the lower back out of it entirely.

exercises.name: DB Reverse Fly
exercises.cue: Light dumbbells. Hinge forward at the hips until your chest is close to parallel with the floor, arms hanging straight down. Lift the dumbbells out to the sides with a soft elbow, leading with the little fingers, until your arms are level with your shoulders. Success looks like: you feel it across the back of the shoulders, not in your lower back or your neck. If you have to swing to move the weight, it is too heavy, and this is one where far too light still works.
exercises.whyHere: the reverse fly goes in the press rest because it pulls the shoulders back while the press pushes them forward

alts.name: Single-Leg RDL
alts.cue: Has sat at 40 lb since May, so this time the weight moves, not just the reps. One dumbbell in the hand OPPOSITE the standing leg. Stand on one leg with the knee slightly bent and frozen. Push the hip backward and let the free leg extend straight behind you like a see-saw, keeping your hips square to the floor: the back hip must not open toward the ceiling. Go until you feel the hamstring stretch, then stand and squeeze. Slow. Touch the bench with your free toe if you lose balance.
alts.whyHere: The single-leg hinge goes in the press rest because it is done standing on one leg with the hips and the press is done sitting down with the arms.

alts.name: BB Romanian Deadlift
alts.cue: The heavy hinge, the one we progress. Breathe IN and tighten your stomach. Bar stays touching your legs the whole way, shins vertical. Bend the knees slightly and then FREEZE them, then push your hips backward toward the wall behind you. Go down until you feel a strong stretch down the back of your thighs, usually around knee height, and no further. Squeeze your bum and snap the hips forward to stand up, breathing out at the top. If your lower back rounds you have gone too far down. STRAPS, because you asked on 18 August: yes, use them, and they will not cost you anything here. Do the first warm-up set with bare hands so you keep noticing what your grip is doing, then strap up for all four working sets. The hamstrings are what this lift is for, and stopping a set because the bar is slipping out of your fingers trains neither. Your grip is not being neglected either: the Farmer Carry on Friday and the Suitcase Carry on Monday are both held bare-handed and that is where grip is meant to be worked. This is standard coaching practice rather than something a trial has tested, so it is a convention, not evidence.

alts.name: B-Stance RDL
alts.cue: Back toe lightly touching the floor for balance, but almost all the weight on the front leg. Much easier to balance, so you can load it heavier.

alts.name: KB Single-Leg RDL
alts.cue: Same movement holding a kettlebell. The handle sits closer to your leg, which some people find easier to control. 8/leg.

alts.name: DB Romanian Deadlift
alts.cue: Two heavy dumbbells in front of your thighs. Same hip push backward, same freeze in the knees.

alts.name: KB Swing
alts.cue: Same hip snap, done fast. Hike the bell back between your legs, then SNAP the hips forward so the bell floats to chest height. Arms do nothing. Start at 35 lb. 2x12.

alts.name: Leg Curl Machine
alts.cue: Lying or seated depending on which machine is free. Set the pad so it sits just ABOVE your heels, on the Achilles, not on your calf. Lie or sit with your knees lined up with the machine pivot, the bolt the arm turns on. Curl your heels toward your bum as far as the machine allows, pause for one second at the tightest point, then lower slowly, taking about twice as long down as up. Success looks like: your hips stay flat on the pad and do not lift as you curl. If they lift, go lighter. This is the only exercise in the week that bends the knee against resistance: every other hamstring movement here is a hinge, where the hamstring works at the hip instead.

alts.name: Cable Reverse Fly
alts.cue: Cables crossed at shoulder height, pull them apart and back.

blocks.why: Ten to fourteen reps against eight to twelve on the other press session, so the same movement is trained light as well as heavy. The single-leg hinge goes in the press rest because it is done standing on one leg with the hips and the press is done sitting down with the arms. Friday used to hold two hinges, the barbell RDL and the single-leg RDL, which is the same pattern twice in one session; the reverse fly goes in the press rest because it pulls the shoulders back while the press pushes them forward.

blocks.label: Horizontal Press

exercises.name: Machine Chest Press
exercises.cue: Your second press of the week, moderate rather than heavy: Tuesday is the day the bench gets pushed. Machine on purpose, so a tired chest does not have to balance dumbbells. Set the seat so the handles line up with the MIDDLE of your chest. Press out until the arms are straight without locking hard, then come back slowly until you feel the stretch. Shoulder blades stay pinned back against the pad.

alts.name: DB Incline Press
alts.cue: SET THE BENCH ONE OR TWO NOTCHES UP FROM FLAT, about 30 degrees, not half way up. This is what you have been doing since at least 28 August and the card was still saying flat, so your logged weights come with you and nothing resets. THE DIFFERENCE, since you asked in the note box: neither one is better. Flat works the middle and lower chest, an incline works the top of the chest and more front shoulder, and they are two halves of the same muscle. The steeper you go the more the shoulder takes over, which is why one or two notches and no more. Success looks like: you feel it across your collarbone rather than under your nipple line. If the shoulders are doing all of it, drop the bench a notch. Feet flat on the floor. Pull your shoulder blades back and down into the bench and keep them there, like you are pinching a pencil between them. Breathe in, lower the dumbbells until you feel a good stretch across the chest, PAUSE for one second so there is no bounce, then press up and breathe out. The dumbbells travel slightly toward each other at the top but do not clang. ADDED 2026-08-22, after he reported feeling this mostly in the triceps and the front of the shoulder: that is usually where the dumbbells are travelling, not how hard you are pushing. Two things to try. Before the first rep, pull your shoulder blades DOWN and TOGETHER into the bench and keep them pinned there the whole set, so your chest is the highest point and the shoulders cannot roll forward. Then press over your LOWER chest, not your collarbone: at the bottom the dumbbells should be beside your nipples with your elbows about halfway between tucked-in and straight-out, and at the top they finish above the same spot rather than drifting toward your face. Success looks like: at the bottom you feel a stretch across the chest, not a pinch at the front of the shoulder. This is standard coaching practice, not a trial finding.

alts.name: Assisted Dip
alts.cue: Lean your chest forward to bias the chest. Enough counterweight for 8 clean reps. You had 5 strict dips in May, so this is trackable.

alts.name: Chest Fly Machine
alts.cue: Elbows slightly bent and fixed, bring the arms together in front of you and squeeze for one second. Stretch, not a press.

exercises.name: Farmer Carry
exercises.cue: Done after the curls rather than alternating with them, because it needs room to walk and the preacher seat does not travel. A heavy dumbbell in each hand, stand as tall as you can, shoulders back, stomach tight, and walk for the seconds shown. Grip, posture and everything down your sides at once. Put them down before your form falls apart, not after. COUNT SECONDS, and type the seconds. Start the watch before you pick the dumbbells up, because you cannot press anything with both hands full. Get to the top of the range on time first, then go heavier.
exercises.whyHere: the carry goes in the press rest: it trains the grip, which pressing does not

alts.name: DB Static Hold
alts.cue: Heavy dumbbells held at your sides, standing still and tall for the seconds shown. Use this when the floor is too crowded to walk.

alts.name: KB Farmer Carry
alts.cue: Kettlebells instead, and THE RACK STOPS AT 50 LB EACH: that is the whole set, 20 up to 50, two of each. His note #18, 2026-08-25: 'Therea no kettlebell after 50 for farmers'. He is right, and it is why the prescribed version is dumbbells, which go to 90 and which he has already carried at 75 per hand. Use this one when the dumbbells are taken, not when you want it heavier. They hang differently and swing a little, so the grip works harder at the same weight.

alts.name: KB Suitcase Hold
alts.cue: One kettlebell in one hand, stand still and tall for the seconds shown. Use this if the floor is too crowded to walk.

alts.name: Suitcase Carry
alts.cue: One dumbbell only. Much harder on the side you are NOT carrying, because it has to stop you leaning. Swap hands each set.

blocks.why: The heavy chest slot, six to nine reps. Nothing else in the week asks the hands to hold on for forty seconds, so the carry goes in the press rest: it trains the grip, which pressing does not. THIS IS THE BLOCK TO DROP IF THE CLOCK BEATS YOU, and the price is that the grip falls from six sets a week to three, under the floor of four.
